PORT CAPACITY- ADDITION WORK 
Recommendation/Observation  
6. The Committee notes that a number of PPP projects involving capacity addition are 
under implementation. The Committee observes that the country's international trade is 
growing fast which warrant s creation of adequate Port infrastructure and capacity. Since 
projects are capital intensive, the resources required to build the Port infrastructure are 
much larger and therefore, public investment has to be supplemented with private sector 
investment in Public Private Partnership (PPP) mode. The Committee desires to be apprised 
as to what extent PPPs have been able to augment resource availability and also minimize 
time overrun and cost escalation in construction of Port projects. The Committee also desires 
to know whether the Model Concession Agreement of 2008 has succeeded in obviating the 
problems faced in execution of PPP projects and make the investment in Port sector 
attractive.             (Para 25) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1. The total capacity of Major Ports was 1452 Million Metri c Ton Per Annum 
(MMTPA) as on 3 1st March, 2019. In addition, a capacity of 21 MMTPA was added during 
the year 2019 -20. This includes the capacity created through PPP projects. Out of this, 27 
PPP projects are under operati on, accounting for total capacity of 239.30 MMTPA. Further, 
there are 22 PPP projects under implementation, accounting for capacity of 227.28 MMTPA. 
Furthermore, the Ministry is working on 12 projects, on PPP basis for augmenting the 
infrastructure of the Major Ports. 
6.2. Few PPP projects have got delayed due to various reasons including delay in 
obtaining statutory / security clearances. These projects are facing project cost issue due to 
delay in implementation. The Ministry has developed guidelines to resolve the cost escalation 
issue in delayed PPP projects. These guidelines were developed by the Ministry in 
consultation with the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance and have been 
circulated to all Major Ports for implementation. Model Con cession Agreement (MCA) is 
formulated considering the business requirements as well as requirements for the 
implementation and maintenance of PPP projects. Several PPP projects have since been 
awarded by Major Ports based on the MCA, 2008 as well as on MCA, 2018. 
6.3. MCA, 2008 giving various parameters for the implementation and maintenance of 
PPP projects, was brought with the following broad objectives:- 
(i) The agreement envisaged an exclusive license to the concessionaire for designing, 
engineering, financ ing, constructing, equipping, operating, and 
maintaining/replacing the project/project facilities and services. 
(ii) The concession period was for a maximum period of 30 years. 

37 
 
(iii) Concession Period begins only after ‘Conditions Precedent’ prescribed in the 
Concession Agreement are met by the Parties within stipulated time limits after 
signing of the Concession Agreement. Two important ‘Conditions Precedent’ to 
be met by the Concessionaire are furnishing of performance guarantee for 
implementing the project and achievement of financial closure. 
(iv) Independent Engineer to be appointed by the Concessioning Authority in 
consultation with the Concessionaire for approving and monitoring design, 
engineering and construction standards for the Project and to issue Comple tion 
Certificate. Change of scope of the project, if initiated by Port, is allowed at the 
cost of the Concessioning Authority during the construction phase. 
(v) Rights and obligations and risk allocation of both the Concessionaire and 
Concessioning Authority t owards operations and maintenance of the Project 
Facilities and providing supporting infrastructure have been spelt out. Commercial 
operation commences on issue of Completion Certificate. 
(vi) User charges, collected by the Concessionaire are regulated by the T ariff 
Authority for Major Ports (TAMP) or such other Competent Authority under the 
Applicable Laws. 
(vii) As consideration for the Concession awarded, the Concessionaire pays to the 
Concessioning Authority License fee towards project site, equipments and other 
assets /utilities taken over from the Concessioning Authority and a share of gross 
revenue earned from the operation of the project as ‘Royalty’. 
(viii) Provisions have been made for remedial measures to be put in place in case of any 
material adverse effect on account of change in law. 
(ix) Provisions made for (a) premature termination of the Concession Agreement in 
the event of a default in meeting the obligations by either Party, after following 
due consultation process & issue of Termination Notice; and (b) for paym ent of 
compensation on such premature termination arrived as per prescribed basis. 
(x) Dispute Resolution Mechanism under the Arbitration Act, 1996 was prescribed. 
(xi) Procedure to be followed for transfer of project site and assets and equipment 
back to the Conce ssioning Authority by the Concessionaire on expiry of the 
concession period, either by premature termination or by efflux of time was laid 
down. 
6.4. Though Public Private Partnership (PPP) mode had been largely successful in Port 
sector, some PPP projects  experienced difficulties during operations, which necessitated a 
review of the MCA, 2008. 

38 
 
6.5. Keeping in view the recommendations of the Committee constituted in February, 
2010, headed by Shri B.K. Chaturvedi , Member (Planning Commission) with Secretary 
(Ministry of Shipping), Finance Secretary, Secretary (Expenditure) and Joint Secretary 
(PMO) as members; Working group; Committee on revising and revitalising PPP model of 
infrastructure (Kelkar Committee); and the experiences gained in managing PPP projects, the 
MCA, 2008 was amended with a view to obviate the problems being faced in execution of 
PPP Projects on account of certain provisions of the present MCA, in order to enhance 
confidence of investors and ma ke the investments in the Port Sector attractive. The salient 
features of the revised MCA, 2018 are as under:- 
(i) Change in equity holding requirements to provide exit route to developers. 
(ii) Payment of royalty by private operators to Port on “per MT of cargo ha ndled” 
basis instead of “% of gross revenue”. 
(iii) Provision for additional land. 
(iv) Improved utilization of project assets and higher productivity. 
(v) Amendment in definition of “Change in Law”. 
(vi) Provision for commercial operation before COD. 
(vii) Provision for mitigation measures - constitution of a Board. 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
6.6. The Committee is concerned to note that some PPP projects have witnessed time 
overruns and cost escalation due to delay in obtaining statutory/security clearances. The 
Committee would like the Ministry to put in place systemic improvements to overcome 
delay in obtaining necessary clearances. The Committee desires to be kept apprised of 
the action taken in this regard. 
 
TRAFFIC HANDLING AT MAJOR PORTS 
Recommendation/Observation  
7. The Committee desires to know whether the negative growth of the traffic handled at 
the 6 Ports is a result of competition from Minor Ports due to their growth rates and huge 
capacity addition through private sector. The Committee also desires to be appri sed of the 
remedial measures taken to arrest this trend.                 (Para 34)   
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1. The Major Ports fall under the jurisdiction of a regulator, the Tariff Authority for 
Major Ports (TAMP).  This results in a lack of a level playing field for Major Ports.  Major 
Ports end up losing business opportunities due to certain tariff related uncer tainties as 

39 
 
determined by TAMP.  Tariffs at non -Major Ports are not regulated, and they price their 
services based on market and competition. 
7.2. The Government has introduced Major Ports Authority Bill in the Parliament to 
provide greater autonomy to Ports.  The proposed bill aims at decentralizing decision making 
and to infuse a professional approach in governance of Ports.  The Bill is aimed at reorienting 
the governance model in central Ports to the landlord Port model in line with the successful 
global practice.  
7.3. The role of Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP) for fixation of the tariff has been 
done away with in the Bill. PPP operators will be free to fix tariffs based on market 
conditions, as notified by the Port Authority. The Board of the Port Authority has been 
delegated the power to fix the scale of rates for other Port services and assets. 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
7.4. The Committee takes cognizance of the fact that the Government has introduced 
the Major Ports Authority Bill in the Parliament which seeks to provide greater 
autonomy to the Major Ports and decentralize decision making. The Committee would 
like the Ministry to pursue vigorously and take the above Bill to its logical conclusion in 
a specified timeframe so that the lack of level playing field for Major Ports is eliminated 
and governance of Major Ports is transformed. The Committee desires to be kept 
updated in this regard.

itself for a targeted action in this regard, so that there is absolute clarity on regulatory 
enforcement of environmental issues and land acquisition and ad -hoc project 
announcements and skewed expenditure pattern are avoided.    
                  (Para: 5.2) 
 
PORT CAPACITY- ADDITION WORK 
The Committee is concerned to note that some PPP projects have witnessed time 
overruns and cost escalation due to delay in obtaining statutory/security clearances. The 
Committee would like the  Ministry to put in place systemic improvements to overcome 
delay in obtaining necessary clearances. The Committee desires to be kept apprised of 
the action taken in this regard.       (Para: 6.6)
          
TRAFFIC HANDLING AT MAJOR PORTS 
The Committee takes cognizance of the fact that the Government has introduced 
the Major Ports Authority Bill in the Parliament which seeks to provide greater 
autonomy to the Major Ports and decentralize decision making. The Committee would 
like the Ministry to pursue vigorously and take the above Bill to its logical conclusion in 
a specified timeframe so that the lack of level playing field for Major Ports is eliminated 
and governance of Major Ports is transformed. The Committee desires to be kept 
updated in this regard.           
                  (Para: 7.4) 
 
CONNECTIVITY TO PORTS 
The Committee notes from the reply that  there is difference of opinion between 
the Ministry of Shipping and Ministry of Road Transport and Highways/NHAI 
regarding fulfillment of certain prescribed conditionalities for execution of connectivity 
projects by NHAI. This does not augur well for speedy execution of these projects. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Inter -Ministerial wrangling should be 
resolved expeditiously at the highest level of Government which should define and spell 
out the future course of action with respect to sanctioned connectivity projects to Ports 
so that there is no disconnect between the Ministries concerned. The Committee desires 
to be kept apprised of the tangible action taken in this regard.     
           (Para: 8.2) 

49 
 
The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should formulate proper 
guidelines and conduct an environmental impact assessment before releasing funds for 
any sanctioned/ s talled/ ongoing project. Therefore, the Ministry of Shipping should 
work in close coordination with Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, NHAI and 
MoEF&CC to address the delay in projects due to land acquisition and environmental 
clearances.           (Para: 8.3) 
 
The Committee feels that the identification of critical projects near Major and 
Minor Ports must also envision the related urbanization and environmental issues of its 
surrounding areas.           (Para: 9.2) 
 
SAGARMALA  
   The Committee is constrained to note that the Ministry has given a generic 
reply to a pointed query of the Committee without elaborating the specific action for 
effective utilization of budgetary allocations for Sagarmala projects. The Committee 
however ho pes that in future the Ministry will process its reply more professionally.                     
                    (Para: 10.2) 
        
DREDGING ACTIVITIES 
The Committee desires to be kept apprised of the further developments in this regard.  
                 
                     (Para: 11.3) 
SHIP BUILDING INDUSTRY 
  The Committee appreciates various steps the Ministry has taken to promote 
indigenous shipbuilding ecosystem in the country. The Committee would however like 
to be apprised of the efficacy of measures initiated.          
                     (Para: 12.2) 
DIRECTORATE GENERAL OF LIGHTHOUSES AND LIGHTSHIPS  
The Committee while making its recommendation had expected the Ministry to 
indicate timelines for implementation of the 23 projects. However,  the action taken note 
is silent in this regard. The Committee observes that setting a timeframe for execution 
of the above projects is important from the point of view of insulating them from cost 
escalation. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a ti meframe be fixed for 
implementation of the 23 projects.        
                          (Para: 13.2) 
INDIAN MARITIME UNIVERSITY 
  
The Committee recommends that the Inland Maritime University, in close 
coordination with Ministry of Shipping, should quickly finalize the proposal for 

50 
 
introduction of new training programmes at IMU’s campuses. The courses so designed 
should be in sync with the changing environment of the maritime sector.        (Para: 14.2) 
          
COCHIN SHIPYARD 
The Committee observes that India’s shipbuilding capabilities have not kept 
pace with its economic development. In order to make Indian Shipyards more 
competitive in the global market, grant of deemed export status for inputs used in 
shipbuilding and ship repair is imperative. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
a decision on granting deemed export status for shipbuilding and ship repair at the 
Cochin Shipyard may be expedited. The Committee desires to be kept apprised of the 
decision in the matter.                     (Para: 15.2) 
The Committee notes the reply and recommends the Ministry to apprise the 
Committee of the policies/ frameworks formulat ed to quicken the process to ensure 
timely completion of ongoing and stalled projects.

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
  
  
ANALYSIS OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2020-21 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
1. The Committee notes that due to broad budgetary cuts imposed by the Ministry of 
Finance, the Ministry has witnessed a reduction in allocation of funds for the Financial Year 
2020-21 and has been allocated only Rs. 2499.83 crore as against its projected dem and of 
Rs. 2647.25 crore.             (Para 23) 
  
Reply of the Ministry 
  
1.1. Factual Statement. Noted by the Ministry. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
2. The Committee notes the submission of the Ministry that the difference in the 
projection made by it and the allocation given for the financial year 2020 -21 is not high and 
that if additional funds are required, it would move the Ministry of Finance for add itional 
allocation at the RE 2020 -21 stage.  The Committee observes that availability of adequate 
resources to the tourism sector is sine qua non for achieving the tourism growth as well as 
inclusive growth.  Since development of tourism infrastructure is capital intensive, the 
Committee apprehends that with the budgetary allocation of Rs.2499.83 crore for 2020 -21, 
which, in the opinion of the Committee, is low, it would be difficult for the Ministry to take up 
significant activities related to on-going infrastructure development of the sanctioned tourism 
circuits/destinations and also development of new tourism products of global standards.  If 
the tourism sector has to play a major role in faster and inclusive growth, the infrastructure 
bottlenecks need to be unleashed.  The Committee notes that more than half of the allocation 
of the Ministry for 2020-21 is devoted for the schemes relating to infrastructure development.  
In most of the States/UTs, the outlay for tourism is meagre and the Central Government  has 
dominance in the domain of public resource mobilization by way of collection of tax revenue. 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry be provided a higher financial outlay at the RE 
2020-21 stage.  The Committee would like the Ministry of Tourism to  bring the above 
recommendation to the notice of Ministry of Finance and also intimate the Committee of their 
response in this regard.             (Para 27) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1. Recommendations of the Committee have been noted for compliance.   The 
recommendations of the Committee have been conveyed to the Ministry of Finance for 

3 
 
necessary action  vide Ministry of Tourism ref . No. G -20017(5) /2019-20 B&A dated 
27.05.2020.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
3. Since the consumption demand arising from tourist expenditure has a multiplier effect 
on the economy, the expansion of the tourist sector can lead to large scale employment 
generation and poverty alleviation. Needless to men tion, tourism has huge potential to 
stimulate overall economic growth and any increase in the outlay for tourism sector can 
propel our country to a faster growth trajectory and will lead to large scale employment 
generation and alleviation of poverty. If o ur country can tap its full potential of the tourism 
sector, it can play a major role for faster and inclusive growth; but for this to happen, the 
budgetary provisions for the Ministry has to be enhanced substantially.  By doing so, tourism 
infrastructure could be strengthened/ upgraded, conservation and development of all 
heritage sites could be undertaken and completed and last mile connectivity to tourist 
destinations could be improved. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government 
should acco rd priority status to the tourism sector and enumerate a fiscal roadmap for 
generating and allocating more financial resource for tourism so that the full potential of a 
vibrant sector could be tapped.          (Para 28) 
Reply of the Ministry 
  
3.1. The recommendations of the Committee have been noted for compliance.  The   
allocation for the tourism Sector is increa sing year after year.   During the Financial Year 
2020-21, Rs. 2499.83 crores have been allotted  to Ministry of Tourism, which is the highest 
ever allocation of fund made to   the Ministry of Tourism.  The BE allocation during 2018-19 
was Rs. 2150 Crore and during 2019 -20 it was Rs. 2189.22 Crore.    From the BE allocation, 
it is evident that the Ministry of Finance is increasing the budgetary out lay for the flagship 
programmes of this Ministry viz., Swadesh Darshan and PRASHAD.  Also, the allocation for 
advertising and publicity to make India a preferred tourist destination is increasing over the 
years.  Further, recommendations of the Committee h ave been conveyed to the Ministry of 
Finance for necessary action.  
  
Recommendation/Observation  
  
4. The Committee notes with dismay the huge mismatch between the projected demand 
for funds and actual allocations made for the Ministry of Tourism for the years 2018 -19 and 
2019-20 as well.  The pattern of shortfall in allocation of funds indicates that budg etary 
requirements are being projected by the Ministry more on the basis of theoretical 
anticipation rather than on actual trend of requirement. The Ministry’s reply that the 
Schemes/Projects undertaken by them are of continuous nature and that the targets  are fixed 
and funds are released as per budgetary allocation by the Ministry of Finance suggests the 
casual and routine manner in which the Budget Estimates are being prepared and the 
Ministry is not very serious about the activities to be undertaken by t hem.  Tourism is 

4 
 
important for both economic growth and employment generation and the corpus of funds 
should not have been arbitrarily decided without reference to any ground reality.     (Para 29) 
  
5. The Committee would, therefore, like the Ministry to have the entire requirement of 
funds realistically assessed after collecting timely information on requirement of funds from 
the State Governments and other stakeholders and take steps to rectify and improve upon the 
existing system of assessing requiremen t of funds. The Ministry should formulate 
Schemes/Programmes which can be implemented in a time -bound manner.  The Committee 
desires to be apprised of the specific action taken in this regard.      (Para 30) 
Reply of the Ministry 
  
5.1. The projection of demands of funds under the schemes are finalized after assessment 
of  the targets set for the ensuing year with realistic approach, position of the approved 
projects under execution, projects under pipeline and requests for the projects received fr om 
the State Governments/ UTs. Further, these are continuing schemes and any shortfall in funds 
due to re duced allocation at RE stage, can be met from the next year’ s budget. It is also 
submitted that during the preceding four years, all funds allocated under various Schemes 
were successfully utilized.  Further, keeping in view the experience gained and challenges 
faced by the Ministry in operation of various Schemes, scheme guidelines f or various 
schemes are amended as and when required.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
6. The Committee takes serious note of the fact that the Ministry has kept the unspent 
provisions of Rs. 43.18 Crore till the close of the financial year 2018 -19 and surrendered the 
same on 29.03.2019 totally disregarding the provisions of General Financial Rules which 
states that unspent provisions in a grant should be surrendered as soon as they are foreseen, 
without waiting for the last day of the year.  The Committee deprecates such a casual 
approach of the Ministry in adhering to the fiscal discipline and desires the Ministry to avoid 
such lapses in future and surrender unspent budgetary provisions timely so that st arved

Recommendation/Observation  
  
18. Cruise Tourism is a supply -driven market and cruise lines are always in search of 
new markets and destinations.  India’s enchanting and exotic destinations could catapult 
India as one of the leading cruise destinations.  But for that to happen, stable and consistent 
operating conditions will have to be concretized because cruise line companies which 
typically plan two to three years ahead, need to know that the basic conditions of operating 
are stable and consistent.  The Committee, therefore, recommends th at the Ministry of 
Tourism in collaboration with Ministry of Shipping should expedite appropriate policy 
measures for developing India’s largely untapped and hitherto small cruise market and pull 
cruise vessels to its shores.  The Committee desires to be u pdated on the progress made in 
this regard.                   (Para 133) 
Reply of the Ministry 
18.1. This Ministry  brought to the notice of Ministry of Shipping about the 
recommendations of the Committee. The reply of Ministry of Shipping is as follow:- 
  

12 
 
(a) The following steps have been taken by the Government to promote Cruise Tourism 
in India: 
i. A delegation comprising  Secretary (Shipping), Chairmen of two cruise ports and 
Economic Advisor, Ministry of Tourism had participated in the Sea Trade Cruise 
Global h eld in Miami in April, 2019.   This forum was utilized to create awareness 
about cruise shipping in India and the various steps taken in this sector for ease of 
doing business. 
ii.  Foreign flag vessels carrying passengers had initially been allowed to call at Indian 
Ports till 5 th February, 2024 without obtaining a licence from Director General of 
Shipping.  This facility has been extended for a further period of 5 years till 
5th February, 2029. 
iii. Standardized Operating Procedures (SOPs) for cruise vessels have b een revised and 
operationalised w.e.f. November, 2017 at all Major Ports. Thereafter a Monitoring 
Committee for implementation of the SOPs was formulated comprising officials from 
Ministry of Shipping, Ministry of Tourism and CISF. 
iv. To address the manpower, coordination and logistic issues, for handling cruise vessels 
at Ports, Port Level Committees with Chairman of respective Major Ports Trust with 
Secretary Tourism of concerned State as Vice -Chairman and Regional Directors of 
respective regions as conveners have been Constituted by Ministry of Tourism. 
v. E-visa facility has been extended to five sea Major Ports namely Mumbai, Goa, 
Mangalore, Cochin and Chennai. Immigration counters have been set up at the 
aforesaid five Major Ports visited by cruise ships.  
vi. To make India attractive to Cruise passengers and to promote cruise tourism in the 
country, Ministry of Home Affairs has at the request of Ministry of Shipping, 
exempted cruise tourists arriving with e -visa from the requirement of biometric 
enrolment for a period of three years i.e. till 31.12.2020 vide their order   20th 
December, 2017.  This will facilitate in expeditious immigration clearance of cruise 
passengers with e-Visa   enabling them to spend more time on shore. 
vii.  The port charges have been reduced a nd all Major Ports are to charge a uniform 
single rate of $0.35 per GRT for first 12 hrs of stay.   Ports will not charge any other 
rate like berth hire, Port dues, pilotage, passenger fee etc from cruise liners.   The 
above rate has been made effective from 3rd November, 2017 and will remain in force 
for a period of three years. 
viii. Concession of 40% on composite port charges of USD 0.35 per GT for 1st 12 hours 
of stay is given to domestic cruise vessels for 75 -100 calls in a year and 50% 
concession for calls ex ceeding 100 in a year for a period of three years i.e. up to 
3.11.2020 (coinciding with validity of composite Port Charges order) at all Major 
Ports except Mumbai  Port, where concession of 20% for 100 calls or more in a year 

13 
 
(1st October to 30 th September) will be applicable. Further extension of this 
rationalisation of tariff for few more years is also being considered and processed. 
ix. The Ports do not levy any priority/ousting/shifting charges for berthing the cruise 
vessel.  
x. Walk-in berthing/ preferential berthing to home port cruises without any extra charge. 
xi. To address manpower, coordination and logistic issues for handling cruise vessels at 
ports, Port Level Committees with chairman of the respective Major Port Trust as 
Chairman, Secretary Tourism of the concerned state as Vice -Chairman and Regional 
Director of the respective region of Ministry of Tourism as Convener have been 
constituted. 
xii. Immigration counters have been set up at five Major Ports visited by cruise ships.   
(b)  In addition, the M inistry has taken up the following tax related issues with the 
Ministry of Finance: 
i. Customs duty exemption on consumption of goods and services on international 
cruise ships when they are in Indian waters and travel from one port to another port to 
ensure a competitive position of India globally and ease of doing business for cruise 
operations in the country. 
ii. Sale of the cruise tickets/ packages attract s GST at a rate of 18% while sale of airline 
ticket attracts GST of 5% for economy class and 12% for other  classes.  On the 
similar lines, the travel by cruise ships is charged at 5% rate for travel in a 
single/double room cabin and 12% for travel by suites. 
iii. The IGST should be exempted on import of cruise vessels in India.   In pre -GST 
regime cruise ships were exempted from customs duty. 
iv. GST may be exempted for goods supplied on board at home Ports for cruise lines to 
promote making Indian ports as home Ports.To stimulate Indians to purchase tickets 
domestically and to retain the profits in India, it is suggeste d that GST on sale of 
international tickets by domestic sale agents be also exempted.

14 
 
19.1. This Ministry brought to the notice of Inland Waterways Authority of India, Ministry 
of Shipping the recommendations of the Committee.   The reply of Inland Waterways 
Authority of India (IWAI) is as follow:- 
(i)        The IWAI Act, 1985, Section I envisages Inland Waterways Authority of India 
(IWAI) is to develop and regulate National Waterways for cargo shipping and 
navigation and thus development of river cruise tourism is not mandated with IWAI. 
However, the infrastructure developed for transportation on National Waterways by 
IWAI include fairway , terminals, jetties, navigation aids etc. They are used by the 
river cruise tourism operators who are from private sector. IWAI’s role is technical 
facilitator. 
(ii)         River cruise tourism has been a regular feature on National Waterway (NW) -
1(Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly river system) and NW -2 (river Brahmaputra) since 
several years. Various cruise operators viz., M/s Heritage River Cruises Pvt. Ltd., M/s

Allahabad to Haldia), NW – 2 (River Brahmaputra from Dhubri to Sadiya), NW -3

Champakara Canals) have already been developed with fairway navigational aids, 
jetties and terminals with mechanized equipment handling facilities for loading and

(iv) In addition to NW -1 & NW -2, NW -3 in Kerala is also a world renowned touris t 
destination for domestic and foreign tourists where house boat tourism with food and 
accommodation facilities are available. The area of operation of these boats includes 
Vembanad lake of Alapuzha, Kuttanad area and Ashtamudi lake of Kollam area in 
NW-3. 
(v)            IWAI under Ministry of Shipping provides navigational channel & assists in 
embarking/ disembarking facility to operators/ passengers. IWAI has 
engaged WAPCOS Limited for preparation of an action plan & detailed road map for 
development of river cruise tourism in India. 
19.2. In a recent initiative, sanction order of Rs 2803.05 lakh dated 19.12.2019 under the 
scheme ‘Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure Development” has been 
issued by ID -Division, Ministry of Tourism for deve lopment of nine main points of

Recommendation/Observation  
 
1. The Committee takes note of the fact that the annual growth rate of the Tourism 
Sector in India is 5.2% and its contribution to GDP is 5.06%. According to UN World 
Tourism Organisation Report (2011), for diversified economies, the contribution of tourism 
to national GDP is over 10% for countries where tourism happe ns to be the main driver of 
national economy. Quite apparently, despite having a strong domestic tourist base which is 
likely to grow further on the back of a rapidly rising middle class with increased disposable 
incomes and having many World Heritage sites and rich fauna, our country has not been able 
to exploit its tourism potential to the fullest possible extent and the tourist sector has not 
proved to be the proverbial engine of growth for our economy. For a country of our size, with 
wealth of attractions and experiences, this underperformance represents significant foregone 
economic value. Since tourism in the country has the potential to emerge as a key economic 
driver through economic growth and employment generation, the country can make a giant 
leap towards achieving 5 trillion dollar economy by tapping the enormous potential of the 
tourism sector. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the strategies adopted for 
promotion and development of the tourist sector should be recalibrated to harness the  full 
potential of Indian tourism and double the current contribution of tourism to GDP in the next 
5 years. The Committee would like the Ministry to prepare a vision document, chalking out a 
road map for accelerating the expansion of the tourism sector an d helping achieve a 5 
trillion dollar economy by 2025 by way of a substantial contribution from the tourism sector. 
The Committee, therefore, desires that policy measures may be initiated by the Ministry to 
accelerate the growth momentum of the tourism sec tor and raise the contribution of tourism 
from the current 5.06% to 10% of GDP.         (Para 32) 
Reply of the Ministry 
  
1.1. Tourism is a rapidly evolving industry that has become increasingly competitive in 
the global arena. It is gaining universal acce ptance as an engine of economic growth and has 
forward and backward linkages with other sectors and ability to create more employment 
opportunities for the disadvantaged sections of the society. In order to realize the full 
potential of the tourism sector,  Ministry of Tourism formulates policies for infrastructure 
development, product development, human resource development, publicity & promotion, 
regulation, research, analysis, monitoring and evaluation, etc. State Governments and the 
private sector act as  the main spring of activities and provide the necessary dynamism and 
speed for implementation of these policies/ schemes to enable the growth and development of 
tourism sector in India.

Recommendation/Observation  
11. The Committee observes that Cruise Shipping is one of the fastest growing 
components of the leisure industry world -wide.  The Indian economy is developing at a 
steady pace and became the fifth largest economy in 2019 surpassing the U.K. and France

disposal incomes is also growing in number. Despite all these advantages, cruise tourism in 
India is still in its nascent stage and India does not even figure in the top ten in As ia in terms

Recommendation/Observation

catering units for Rs. 15.80 crore . The Committee observes that renovation and upgradation

match the standards of the private players, ITDC would require more funding support from

The Hotel Ashok to be taken up on PPP basis by DIPAM, the proposal for any major 
renovation of Ashok has been put on hold. However, the works of repair and maintenance

during current F.Y. 2020-21.

Recommendation/Observation

with previous two rounds. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of 
Tourism, in coordination with the Ministry of Civil Aviation, and through the Inter -

operationalisation of these 36 tourist routes/sectors.  The Committee would like to be 
apprised of the progress made in this regard.                 (Para 146)

important tourist destinations, to the Ministry of Civil Aviation. The Ministry of Civil

2.1     The observations of the Committee are noted.  
 
OUTLAY 2020-21: Demands vis-à-vis Allocations 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.  The Committee notes that the gap between the projected requirement of the Ministry 
and the amount allocated by the Ministry of Finance has further widened to about 40% of 
the projected requirement at BE stage in 2020 -21, as against a gap of 34.5% and 22.5% 
at RE stage in 2018 -19 and 2019-20 respectively. The Committee hopes that the Ministry 
of Road Transport and Highways is able to carry out its pro jects and schemes by 
considering the inter -se priorities of its projects. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry should strive to ensure that the quality of the Ministry’s projects is not 
compromised due to availability of limited funds. 
(Para 34) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1     The concerns of the Committee are noted. All efforts shall  be made to ensure that 
quality of implementation of projects is not compromised. Further, additional fund 
requirements, if any, shall be appropriately projected under RE 2020-21. 

3 
 
 
ROAD DEVELOPMENT 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.  The Committee is of the view that the efficiency of Highway alignment in Greenfield 
projects is much higher than Brownfield projects. The Committee recommends that as per 
the policy of MoRTH, linear road construction and Greenfield projects should be 
accorded utmost priority for construction of road projects. 
(Para 41) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1     Majority of the existing Road projects have been developed in the past with 
connectivity of enroute towns as the key consideration. This has led to sub -optimal 
alignments, involving longer routes to be covered between major destinations. Longer 
the route, h igher is the cost and time involved in traversing the length of the Highway, 
which also entails associated environmental costs. There is a feasibility of completely 
new alignments, following crow -flight concept to the extent feasible, which reduces the 
distance between two major connectivity (Origin and Destination) points. The Ministry 
has issued guidelines dated 26.02.2018 for the DPR Consultants in this regard.  
4.2    Under Phase -I of Bharatmala Pariyojana, about 5,871 km length of Greenfield 
corridors have been identified for development. Out of these , projects in about 1,645 km 
have been awarded. Balance lengths are targeted to be awarded by FY 2021 -22.   
 
Recommendation/Observation 
5.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensure the inclusion of provision 
for service roads on both sides across the National Highways network. The Committee 
feels that important roads with significant traffic load, such as Hyderabad -Kurnool 
Tollgate to Bengaluru Route Tollgate and other such toll gates, s hould be given priority. 
The Committee feels that this would allow smooth passage of city traffic as well as slow 
speed vehicles and lower the number of road accidents happening on the National 
Highways. 
(Para 42) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1     The service roads are provided only at urban/ semi -urban locations on NHs where 
local traffic is substantial and as such service roads are provided on a small length of 
NHs. 
5.2   However, as per the extant policy, for NH stretches developed to 6 -lane NH 
standards, th e service roads are provided in continuous length on both sides; unless 
otherwise specified for a project, the continuity is broken at locations of major bridges, 
at locations of toll plazas in a length of one km, in areas where no cross traffic or access 
traffic is expected provided the length of such section is at least one km. However, 
service roads may not be provided where there is no settlement or road side 
development abutting the Project Highway or the connecting roads are spaced more than 
2 km. 

4 
 
5.3   Service Road in a length of 40.838 Km has already been provided on NH -44 in 
Thondupally to Kurnool city section. Further, NHAI has also invited bids for 
construction of service road on both side from km.204.800 to 205.800 in Kurnool city 
for ensuring sa fety to local road users.  
 
MAINTENANCE AND REPAIR OF NATIONAL HIGHWAYS 
Recommendation/Observation 
6.   The Committee strongly rec ommends that  a mechanism should be es tablished to 
periodically monitor the quality of Highways. A policy fra mework should be set in place 
to ensure that  repair works and maintenan ce of Highways are carried out within  a 
prescribed tim eframe so  as to ens ure certain minimum  standards of pliability on t he 
Highways. 
(Para 46) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1    Regional Officers of the Ministry in consultation with concerned State PWDs 
continuously monitor the condition of National Highways and works on National 
Highways requiring maintenance and repair are taken up for execution as and when 
required to keep the highways in traffic worthy condition.  
6.2      Ministry has issued a guideline making the uses of Network Survey Vehicles 
(NSVs) mandatory. These vehicle s, besides collecting data related to road inventory will 
also help in capturing relevant data related  to the quality and serviceability condition of 
the NHs. 
6.3    A mechanism to measure the health condition of roads has been developed & the 
provisions of equipment -based monitoring, using NSVs, Falling Weight Deflectometer 
(FWD), Mobile Bridge Inspection  Unit (MBIU) etc. at specified intervals, have been 
incorporated in the consultancy agreements for all projects under implementation and 
Operations & Maintenance.   
6.4    Policy decisions were taken in August, 2018 to increase the concurrent defects 
liability cum maintenance periods for projects implemented on EPC mode to 5 years & 
10 years for flexible (bituminous) pavements and rigid (cement concrete) pavements 
respectively. Thus, EPC contractor is made responsible for concurrent maintenance and 
rectification of defects during the above -mentioned enhanced periods of 5/ 10 years as 
are relevant. This is expected to make Maintenance & Repair (M&R) of NHs more 
systematic and organized.  
6.5    As already mentioned, the Ministry has recently taken policy decisi on to allow 
booking / reimbursement of expenditures for ordinary / petty repairs carried out in a 
Financial Year (FY) as a spill over commitment on subsequent FY. This is expected to 
improve efficiency of booking of expenditure.  
6.6    The concerns of the Committee have been noted and the Ministry shall take all 
necessary actions towards ensuring proper M&R of NHs and better pliability of NHs.

lags behind in terms of length of Expressways. The Committee feels that Expressways are 
a crucial infrastructure requirement to ensure fast and seamless connectivity between the 
economic hubs of the country, as a l arge amount of  cargo and pa ssengers across  the 
country trav el by road. The Committee recommends the Ministry to work  out plans for  
more E xpressways in the country. Special attention be given to road quali ty and safety 
standards on Expressways since the vehicles travel at a fast speed and with low reaction 
time available to the drivers, wherein even the slightest fault in the road geometrics could 
lead to fatal accidents. 
(Para 60)

remaining 2,338 km, 659 km has already been awarded till 30th April 2020. Out of the 
remaining 1,6 79 km balance for award length, 1531 km will be targeted for award in the 
current Financial Year.

amount proportionate to the over -loading weight can be determined through the Weigh -
in-Motion system at the lane level or Static Weigh Bridge system near the plaza vicinity 
and can be handed over to the vehicle user. Thereafter, the exce ss fee or the challan 
amount can be paid in cash or other modes of payments at the fee plaza or collected 
through any other mechanism as provisioned.  
30.3    However, considering the fact that the penalty/challan amount is usually much 
more than the appli cable fee therefore it is proposed that same may not be deducted

increase number of blacklisted FASTags.

9.  The Committee notes that after a sudden spike in private investments in 2015-16, the 
Ministry has not been able to replicate its s uccess in the  following years. The Com mittee 
recommends that given the cru cial need for private investment in the road infrastructure 
sector, the Ministry may look into the reasons behind the declining private interest and 
work out solutions to regain the same. 
(Para 75) 
10.  The  Committee notes the declining private sector investment for the road sector 
and fe els that increasing the Gross Budgetary Support every year is not suitable for 
sustained gr owth. The Committee, ther efore, recommends that viable measures may  be 
taken to rekindle private sector interest in road infrastructure sector.  
(Para 76) 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1     There has been a sharp decline in the private sector participation due to failure of 
projects awarded during 2010 -11 & 2011 -12. Thereafter, Ministry decided to award 
works on EPC Mode and there was decline in the participation of private sector in road 
projects. Thereafter, a new mode of contract for reviving the participation of private 
sector i.e. Hybrid Annuity Mode (HAM) was introduced. This is expected to increase 
participation of private sector in road projects. Besides, a new mode i.e. TOT has also 
been introduced last year. Under TOT, two packages have been bid out successfully.

The response is encouraging. To revive BOT Mode in Highway sector, meetings at 
various levels involving stakeholders have been conducted and modifications in the 
Model Conces sion Agreement have been initiated. All the above steps are expected to 
increase participation of private sector to the desired level.  
10.2   Further, steps to amend the Model Concessionaire Agreement (MCA) of BOT 
(Toll) Document have already been taken so  as solve the reasons behind the declining 
private interest. Meetings of Inter -Ministerial Group were held and thereafter the draft 
modified MCA was placed on website for consultations of the stakeholders. Draft 
Modified MCA was further modified and therea fter meeting of Inter -Ministerial Group 
also took place. The modified MCA is in advanced stages of preparation.  
10.3   Also, NHAI is planning to launch its first InvIT also by 30 th September 2020 so as 
to mobilise small savings in the form of units in addi tions to mobilise funds of 
Institution/sovereign funds of foreign countries. This shall be all in addition to 
monetisation of road assets in the form of TOT.

INCREASING DEBT OF NHAI 
Recommendation/Observation 
13.  The Committee is concerned to note that the amount of debt NHAI has to repay as on 
date, is more than twice the present annual budgetary allocation of the  Ministry of 
Road Transpo rt and Highways. The debt servicing cost is estimated to rise up to Rs. 
34,846 crore in the FY 2021 -22 and w ould continue to be a si zeable figure in the 
following years. The Com mittee fe els that the NHAI  needs to take  urgent proactive 
measures to solve i ts finan cial issues. The Co mmittee r ecommends that the Ministry 
should constitu te an Advis ory Commi ttee, to l ook into the issues  pertaining to the 
increasing debt of NHAI and the efficacy of the measures being taken by the Ministry and 
NHAI, in order to monetize their assets, to come out of the present debt trap. The 
Committee further recommends that the Ministry may consider the  feasibility of 
implementing strong  measures such as hiking  the toll charges across the country and 
postponing certain projects to later dates, since the present financial health of NHAI 
is not su stainable in the long run and would create bi gger i ssues in the r oad 
infrastructure sector in the future. 
(Para 90) 
Reply of the Ministry 
13.1     In order to reduce the debt liability in future and to monetize the assets, NHAI is 
exploring the possibility of raising funds by forming SPV. This will help NHAI to keep 
the funds so raised, off balance sheet of NHAI.

 Also Training sessions are conducted for NHAI officials & 
IE/AE/Supervision Consultant in order to facilitate them for proper 
monitoring of Road Safety Standards. 
 Road Safety Audit is being conducted by NHAI before, during and post 
construction for adherence to road safety standards.  
 The Road Safety Audit recommendations submitted by Safety 
Consultants are communicated to concerned concessionaires/ contr actors 
for ensuring the implementation of these recommendations. 
 Each blackspot location is being inspected by Officers of Regional 
Offices, State PWDs/ RCDs (for stretches entrusted with State 
Governments), Project Director of Concerned PIU and Road Safet y 
Expert of the Independent Engineers (IE)/ Authority’s Engineers (AE) 
/Safety Consultants and recommend the mitigation measures.   
 Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019 has been enforced since 
01.09.2019; these have new provisions as (1A) of section 116, ( 1A) of 
Section 138 etc., regarding Road Safety. 

36 
 
 Safety measures are being taken during construction by the respective 
concessionaire as per IRC guidelines and CA provisions and as per the 
suggestions/recommendations of safety expert of I.E or Safety Consul tant 
engaged for the respective project stretches. 
 Safe crossing facilities such as construction of VUP’s, PUP’s, FOB’s, 
service road, etc. are also being considered wherever required under 
safety reasons for the stretches under NHAI, based on recommendati ons 
of the standing committee consisting of Project Director, RSE of 
Independent Engineer, concerned local police authority and RSO of the 
RO, under delegation powers of RO vide circular No.1.1.27 dated 
20.03.2018. 
 Further, road safety week is conducted ev ery year to create safety 
awareness among the road users and also in various schools, villages/local 
public, and eye check -up camps for drivers etc., to reduce and prevent 
accidents.  
 For completed projects, Incident Management team is deployed at Toll 
Plazas on Highways consisting of Ambulances, Route Patrol Vehicles and 
Tow away cranes to provide medical help to victims as quickly as 
possible. 
 Paramedic with required equipment are mobilized for ambulance as per 
IRC guidelines/NHAI Extant Policy Circular issued from time to time. 
 The mobile app “Sukhad Yatra” has been developed which is used to 
provide the information related to Toll Plaza through GPS location and 
also implemented NHAI’s 24 X 7 Toll Free helpline number – 1033 for 
any incidence/emergency on  National Highways. Further, display boards 
(installed retro reflectorized sign boards) in this regard as per IRC codal 
provisions has been fixed on National Highways. Ambulances are 
equipped with Automatic vehicle tracking system with GPS technology 
for tracking vehicle’s current location.

28.  The Committee feels that one of the major reasons behind road accidents is the poor 
condition of roads. Presence of potholes can prove to be fatal, even more so in the rainy 
season. The  Committee re commends that the Mini stry may make provisions for  speedy 
redressal of s afety concerns on  National Hi ghways. The Committee fe els that  given the 
vast stretches of National Highways in the country, allowing road users to report potholes, 
lack of lighting, and other safety concerns through the use of smartphone application 
would be very helpful to rec eive info rmation on  such issues, along with pin point 
location. The Ministry/NHAI m ay then fo rward the  complaints received to the  
concessionaire, responsible for the maintenance of the concerned road. User feedback may 
also be sought on resolution of the reported issue. The Com mittee desires that such 
solutions may be implemented and sufficient fund be provided for that purpose. 
(Para 189) 
Reply of the Ministry

28.1     Pre-monsoon repair and maintenance of the stretches is being carried out on NHs 
through Concessionaire/ Contractor/ Agency through Open Competitive Bidding to 
ensure safer roads. The rectification of the potholes is taken at the top p riority. While 
during construction period Concession/Contract Agreements provide the specific 
provisions for all maintenance activities that shall be carried out by the Concessionaire 
under their obligations.  e.g. Article 12.4 under Concession Agreement of  Hybrid 
Annuity Projects states that “ During the Construction period ,the Concessionaire shall 
maintain ,at its cost ,the existing Project Highway to ensure that the road is in pothole 
free condition…” The response time for potholes is 48 hours. The respo nse time for 
lighting defects is 24 hours for any major failure of the system while it is only 8 hours 
for faults and minor failures. The resources should be accordingly allocated for such top 
class protocol to have world class roads.  
28.2   Complaints re garding maintenance can be lodged by users on toll free no. 1033. 
Reporting of Potholes is already included in the “Sukhad Yatra” Mobile App.

ANNUAL PLAN 2019-20 
The Committee is concerned to note the pattern of low spending under several key 
Heads, especially Maintenance & Repair (M&R). The Committee observes that the 
projected requirement of the Ministry for M&R for  FY 2019 -20 was Rs. 6,500 
crores, but the Ministry could not utilize even the allocated amount of Rs. 2,000 
crores. The Committee urges the Ministry to avoid such ritualistic allocations which 
remain on paper only and recommends that the Ministry should ma ke all out efforts 
to ensure optimum fund utilization under all the major Heads, laying special focus 
on the Maintenance & Repair Head. 
(Para 1.10) 
 
The Committee notes that the Ministry has merely chosen to note its observations 
for compliance and no specific mention has been made or details furnished of the 
initiatives taken by the Ministry to resolve the issues that are presently preventing 
the Ministry from ensuring optimum utilization of funds. The Committee, therefore, 
urges upon the Ministry to t ake concrete steps to ensure balanced expenditure of 
funds allocated to the Ministry in all the quarters of a Financial Year.  
(Para 2.2) 
 
The Committee terms the reasons furnished by the Ministry as routine in nature. 
The Ministry has been casual in its a pproach while launching these projects without 
making any assessment as to actual fund requirements and the corpus of fund seems 
to have been arbitrarily decided without reference to ground realities. The 
Committee would like the Ministry to be proactive w hile tackling the issues causing 
slow pace of expenditure, since delays in infrastructure projects cause significant 
cost overruns over period of time.  
(Para 4.3) 
 
The Committee is not convinced by the reasons furnished by the Ministry for under -
utilization of funds for Maintenance & Repair, Research & Development and Road 
Transport Heads. The Committee opines that instead of surrendering funds 
allocated to M&R for enhancing matching allocation to NH(O) Head, the Ministry 

83 
 
should have examined the reasons t hat led to low expenditure under this Head and 
strived to resolve them. The Committee observes that the funds are released to the 
States under M&R and R&D schemes on the basis of fulfillment of certain 
conditionalities by the State Governments/ implementin g agencies, such as 
submission of Utilization Certificates and Audited Statements, regularization of 
expenditures, completion of pre-construction activities, etc. Some of the States could 
not fulfill the conditions prescribed. The Committee is constrained to note that apart 
from administrative failure of the recipient States in fulfilling the conditions, the 
Ministry is also not in a position to estimate the extent of utilization of allotted sums 
and examine the feasibility of attaining the mandatory condit ions by the States. 
Taking the above into consideration, the Committee would like the Ministry to 
review the conditions and make them more flexible in order to enable the States to 
fully utilize the Grants. The Committee would also recommend to the Ministr y to 
enter into Memorandum of Understanding with the recipient States so as to act in a 
coordinated manner to overcome the shortcomings in utilization of budgeted funds.  
(Para 6.8) 
 
The Committee notes that the debt repayment obligations of NHAI are incre asing 
every year. The specific concern expressed by the Committee has been on the 
reasons for lower IEBR projection for 2020 -21 as compared to RE 2019 -20 IEBR of 
Rs. 75,000 crores. The ATN is devoid of any such details. The Committee, therefore, 
desires to  be apprised of the precise reasons in this regard. The Committee also 
recommends that the Ministry should strive to set higher targets for IEBR in the 
upcoming financial year so as to lower the strain on the budgetary resources of the 
Government.  
(Para 7.2) 
 
The Committee notes that an outlay of Rs. 91,823.22 crore has been earmarked for 
the development, maintenance and management of 11,000 km of National Highways 
and roads in 2020-21 and hopes have been pinned on higher  budgetary allocation at 
RE stage. The Committee observes that the expected higher allocation at RE stage is 
hitched to higher GDP which may, however, not materialize due to a deceleration in 
the growth rate of the Indian economy on account of global and domestic slowdown 
in the wake of Co vid-19 pandemic and the resultant shortfall in tax collection. The 
Committee would therefore recommend to the Government to create an exclusive 
corpus with lending shortfall meant for the highway and road infrastructure sector 
under priority sector landing.  
(Para 8.4)

the 2000 km length of  coastal and port connectivity roads identified for BM Phase -I 
is directly linked with the performance of the Shipping sector of the country and 
thus, all efforts must be made by the Ministry to resolve the bottlenecks causing 
delay in this project.  
(Para 26.4) 
 
ECONOMIC CORRIDORS AND STRATEGIC HIGHWAYS 
The Committee notes the progress made by NHAI and NHIDCL in this regard. The 
Committee is of the view that a large portion of the length targeted under 
Bharatmala Pariyojana Phase-I has not even been awarde d yet, and thus, it is likely 
to miss the completion target set for 2021 -22. The strategic importance of Border 

88 
 
and International connectivity roads cannot be overstated. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should make all necessary efforts to keep the 
completion of development of the Border and International connectivity roads on 
track.  
(Para 27.2) 
 
DELAYS IN ROAD PROJECTS 
The Committee takes note of the various efforts being made by the Ministry to 
minimize delays in its road projects. However, it  is clear from the major delays 
noticed in majority of road projects that the efforts of the Ministry are not yielding 
the required results. Delays in road projects not only cause significant inconvenience 
to the road users but create avoidable stress on t he financial health of the Ministry, 
as well as the sectors dependent on road connectivity in a particular region. In light 
of this, the Committee reiterates the recommendation made in Para 178 of its 278 th 
Report on Demands for Grants (2020 -21) of Ministr y of Road Transport and 
Highways seeking establishment of a Special Delay Mitigation Cell dedicated to 
address delays in ongoing road projects of the Ministry.  
(Para 28.9) 
 
Noting that no action seems to have been taken on creation of a dedicated body wit h 
the sole objective of minimizing and mitigating delays in the various projects of the 
Ministry, the Committee reiterates the recommendation made in Para 28.9 in 
Chapter III of this Report.  
(Para 29.2) 
 
CO-ORDINATION WITH STATE GOVERNMENTS 
The Committee appreciates that the existing schemes are being implemented by the 
Ministry in co -ordination with State Governments to bolster their public transport 
system. The Committee further desires that the Ministry may work out a scheme to 
provide special financial  as well as technical support, wherever possible, to public 
transportation systems for the States which tackle issues related to high pollution 
every year.  
(Para 30.4) 
 
STAFFING IN NHAI 
The Committee notes with concern that NHAI is still grappling with large number of 
vacant posts. For overcoming the problem, NHAI has initiated certain measures 
which include revision of Recruitment Rules, filling vacancies on direct and 

89 
 
deputation basis, etc. The Committee apprehends that these measures might not be 
enough to tide over the issue of shortage of manpower in the short term. The 
Committee would therefore recommend that NHAI may explore the avenue of 
engaging skilled manpower on contract basis to address the problem of shortage of 
skilled manpower.  
(Para 31.4) 
 
MISCELLANEOUS 
CAG Report on Hyderabad-Bengaluru Toll Road 
The Committee desires to know the course of action being planned by NHAI in the 
light of the balance in the Escrow Account being insufficient for recovery of the 
damages. The Committee may also be apprised of the action taken by the Ministry / 
NHAI to ensure that such cases do not recur in the future.  
(Para 32.2) 
 
Public Project Monitoring Facility 
The Committee appreciates the initiative taken by NHAI for publication of 
information about its projects on its website ( https://nhai.gov.in/project-website.htm). 
The Committee, however, notes that several key columns are yet to be updated in 
respect of the projects displayed on this webpage. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that information regarding concessionaires working on the projects 
and details of officer(s) responsible for ensuring desired quality for a particular 
project, may also be published on the project details page.  
(Para 33.5) 
 
Promotion of Electric Vehicles in the country 
The Committee is of the view that electric vehicles are going to be ubiquitous in the 
near future, given their economic as well as environmental benefits. The Committee 
would like to know the reasons for deferring the proposal for exemption of 
registration fees for battery operated/ electric vehicles. The Committee feels that 
exempting registration fees for electric vehicles will give a boost to the demand for 
such vehicles in the country. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, in close 
co-ordination with other Ministries concerned, should strive for setting up the 
necessary infrastructure for this inevitable transition. The demand thus created, will 
also push domestic vehicle manufacturers to start giving more importance to this up 
and coming segment.  The Committee notes that countries like Norway, besides 
granting exemption from vehicle acquisition tax and several other incentives, even 
went to the extent of exempting electric vehicles from toll taxes. As a result of such 
incentives, more than 50% of new car sales in Norway are now electric vehicles. The 

90 
 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may examine the electric vehicles policies 
being adopted worldwide as well as Delhi Electric Vehicles Policy, 2020 and come 
out with a lucrative electric vehicle policy with a view to promote/ incentivize the 
adoption of electric vehicles in the country.  
(Para 34.2) 
 
Coordination with Local Police Departments 
The Committee notes the reply. The Committee, however, feels that the above 
mentioned policy of the Minist ry to not permit erection of check barriers on 
National Highways except in certain situations mentioned in their reply, is not 
actually implemented on ground since vehicles being stopped for checking of 
documents is a common sight, even on National Highway s. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry may write to all the State Governments to 
intimate/ remind them about the relevant policy in this regard.  
(Para 35.3) 
 

91

OF THE MINISTRY IS STILL AWAITED 
 
EARMARKING OF OBLIGATED ALLOCATIONS FOR SCHEDULED CASTE 
SUB PLAN (SCSP) AND TRIBAL SUB PLAN (TSP) 
The Committee agrees with the observation made by the Ministry that given the type 
of infrastructure work carried out by the Minist ry, it is not feasible to adopt the 
approach for dedicated earmarking of funds under SCSP component. The 
Committee may be apprised of the response received from NITI Aayog, DEA and

Jawaharlal Nehru Port 
PORT PERFORMANCE 
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee notes the increased efficiency of the Port in terms of containers handled 
at 0.43% and the increase in average output per ship Berth day overall at 1.50% over the 
previous years.  The Committee commends the ef ficient management of the Port authorities in  
improving the efficiency parameters of the Port in order to make it as competitive as some of the 
best ports in the world.                           (Para 64)              
2. The Committee applauds the steps ta ken to improve the infrastructure facilities of JNPT 
and would urge upon the Government to further upgrade and modernize the Port to assure 
improved performance benchmarking against global standards.           (Para 67) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The improv ement in the performance has continued in the year 2018 -19 also. During 
Apr.-Dec., 2018, the total traffic handled at port was up by 7.39% as compared to same period of 
last year. The Output Per Shipberth day was also up by 3.7%. The vessel pre -berthing detention 
and turnaround time have come down by 18.5% & 5.75% respectively.  
2.2 The Port has undertaken series of projects to enhance the capacity and upgrade facilities 
to ensure improved performance. The project under implementation stage includes:  
 Construction of Coastal Berth: Dedica ted facility for coastal cargo out of custom bound area 
with separate approach road.   
 Capital Dredging work: To facilitate berthing of larger container vessels with deeper draft.   
 Construction of SEZ: To provide impetus for development of port based industry. 

3 
 
 Parking Plaza: The facility for direct entry of factory stuffed containers with in Customs 
Processing Zone.  
 Dry Ports at Jalna & Wardha: To connect hinterland directly with Port. 
 Widening of roads:  widening of Port roads connecting national highways.

VOC Port Trust 
TRAFFIC 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. Moreover, the Committee feels that the proximity of P orts, both private and major, alon g 
the coast, cater to the same hinterland. The number of P orts is far larger than the demand for 
them. The supply exceeds the demand and this has resulted in the underutilization of the 
economies of scale. The Committee fails to understand the lack of plan ning and foresight in the 
operation of this port and the neglect of the Port by the Ministry of Shipping  and the State 
Government.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Shipping must focus its 
attention on the development of the Port a s a transshipment hub. The Committee recommends 
that the Port must reduce its reliance on bulk cargo in terms of coal etc. and change its business 
model in order to attract more varied traffic.            (Para 124) 

4

Emerging Constellation of Container Terminals in South India 
Recommendation/Observation  
8. Investment in smaller new Ports in India can yield much better returns as they would 
service vessels on coastal and inland waterway. The Committee feels that the three ports coming 
up within a distanc e of about 130 nautical miles need to be developed and strategized in such a 
manner that all the three receive sufficient cargo to ensure profitable operations. The Committee 
thus recommends that infrastructure development of one port should not be at the cost of the 
development of another nearby port.             (Para 246) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 Observations of the Committee have been noted. 
Recommendation/Observation  
9. The Committee recommends that efforts must be concentrated on the development and  
expansion of infrastructure that would make water transport more attractive, instead of 
prioritizing road transport and turn already over -crowded highways into death traps. More 

9 
 
emphasis must be placed on the coast route and inland waterways as a mode of transport for 
hinterland cargo connectivity and its development must be made a priority.       (Para 247) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1 Government declared 111 (including 5 existing and 106 new) National Waterways 
(NWs) spread over 24 states under the National  Waterways Act, 2016, which came into effect 
from 12 April, 2016 to promote Inland Water Transport (IWT) in the country.  
9.2 Out of these 111 waterways, NWs – 1, 2 and 3 are operational and cargo and passenger 
vessels are moving on them. The development works on NW-4 under Phase-I had commenced in 
2017 and pre-project activities have been initiated on NW-5.   
9.3 In addition, Government is implementing the Jal Marg Vikas Project (JMVP) at an 
estimated cost of Rs. 5369.18 crore for capacity augmentation of navigation on National 
Waterway-1 (NW -1) on the Haldia – Varanasi stretch of Ganga -Bhagirathi- Hooghly River 
System with the technical and financial assistance of the World Bank. The salient features of the 
project are construction of three multimodal term inals at Haldia (West Bengal), Sahibganj 
(Jharkhand), Varanasi (U.P.) and two intermodal terminals at Kalughat (Bihar), Ghazipur (U.P.); 
five pairs of Ro -Ro terminals at Rajmahal (Jharkhand) -Manikchak (West Bengal), Samdaghat 
(Jharkhand)-Manihari (Bihar), Kahalgaon-Tintangha (Bihar), Hasnapur -Bakhtiyarpur (Bihar),  
Buxer (Bihar)-Saraikota (U.P.); and  one new navigational lock at Farakka (West Bengal). JMVP 
is scheduled to be completed in March, 2023. 
9.4. Based on the outcome of techno -economic feasibility and Detailed Project Reports 
(DPRs) prepared for new 106 NWs, technical interventions are being planned for safe navigation 
and shipping on technically viable NWs. As per the DPRs completed so far for the new NWs, 36 
NWs have been found to be technically viable.  
Cargo Evacuation from Indian Ports in Terms of Transport Mode 
Recommendation/Observation  
10. Furthermore, the Committee recommends that evacuation of cargo to and from the port 
areas have to be properly synchronized so that the inter -modal network  functions smoothly. 
Road and rail connectivity form an integral part of the port infrastructure as inefficient 

10 
 
evacuation of cargo can undermine the entire operation of a port. In particular, containerization 
of cargo presupposes a seamless link with the road and rail network in an ‘end to end’ transport 
system. Congestion at ports results in delayed evacuation of cargo due to inadequate road and 
rail capacity. This adversely impacts the competitiveness of Indian industry. Port connectivity 
has ramifications that go beyond the operation of a port per se.          (Para 252) 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1 Observations of the Committee have been noted. 
Cabotage Laws 
Recommendation/Observation  
11. The Committee recommends that a study must be conducted on the eff ects of Cabotage 
Laws in the shipping sector of the country. The Committee feels that research must be conducted 
as to why, given the reduction of the Cabotage laws, the Ports have witnessed a paltry level of 
transshipment. The policy of the Ministry in th is regard must be scientifically monitored and 
solutions to the same must be devised. The Committee extends its full cooperation in this matter 
as it feels that the success of transshipment hubs in the country is essential for the growth of 
Ports in India.                (Para 261) 
Reply of the Ministry 
11.1 Effects of relaxation of Cabotage laws are regularly being monitored particularly impact 
on transshipment. As per the recent trends (u pto December, 2018), the transshipment details are 
given as under: 
a.   The number of Indian EXIM containers handled in India has increased from 6.4 Million 
TEUs in April – December FY16 TO 7.9 Million TEUs in April – December FY19. 
b.  The overall container traffic in Indian ports has increased from 99 MMT in April – 
December FY16 to 126 MMT in April – December FY19 at a CAGR OF 8% in the backdrop of 
this, the growth of containers transshipped in Indian ports has increased by 33% CAGR in the 
same period indicating a significant increase in share of Indian ports in transshipment. 

11 
 
c.  The growth in container transshipment through Indian ports was 26% in tonnage terms 
and 25% in TEUs terms during April – December, 2018 against the corresponding period of last 
year. 
11.2 Overall, India aims to reduce transshipment of its contai ners at foreign ports such as 
Colombo, Singapore, Jebel Ali, etc, in order to reduce logistics costs for Indian traders and time 
and conserve valuable foreign exchange for the country, while simultaneously supporting 
economic growth and jobs in India that would otherwise be lost to other countries that handle 
Indian cargo during transshipment. 
11.3 Shipping lines do their route planning on an annual basis at the very least and changing 
schedule of services along with accompanying partners requires careful p lanning and operational 
management by them. It takes 2 to 3 years from commencement to firmly establish 
transshipment and hence the effect of recent cabotage relaxation by India coupled with an 
infrastructure push, rationalization of tariffs, procedure sim plification (such as inter -terminal 
transfer), etc, is expected to take some time to manifest.

Efficiency of the Port Sector Operations 
Recommendation/Observation  
15. The Committee feels that low productivity and high vessel turnaround t ime at Indian 
ports are due to: (i) Low level of mechanization and insufficient draft; (ii) Skewed handling 
capacity for different types of cargo; and (iii) Infrastructure constraints in hinterland 
connectivity. It has been observed that lagging behind oth er countries on performance 
parameters pushes up the cost of trade and renders Indian ports less competitive. Non -Major 
Ports have fared well, ensuring quicker turnaround by investing in the infrastructure to handle 
larger vessels. Considering the strategic location of India’s Major Ports and their importance to 
trade, there is an opportunity to improve their performance to meet global benchmarks. Most of 
the Major Ports have high Turnaround Time  even while the utilization level is low and only a 
few have the ability to handle bigger cape -size vessels. The shipping industry is moving towards 
cape-size vessels. So, it is important that India develops cape handling capability at its key ports 
to ensure economics of scale for the trade.             (Para 231) 
Reply of the Ministry 
15.1 While increasing the capacity of major ports, Ministry of Shipping  has been striving to 
improve the operational efficiencies through mechanization, digitization and process 
simplification. The Average Turnaround Time during 2018 -19 improved to 59.85 Hrs from 
96.00 Hrs during 2014 -15. The Average Output Per Ship Berthday has increased from 12458 
Tonnes in 2014-15 to about 16434 Tonnes during 2018-19.   
15.2 Ministry of Shipping had identified various parameters under Ease of Doing B usiness for 
reducing dwell time and transaction costs in the Major Ports. These include elimination of 
manual forms, accommodation for laboratories to Participating Government Agencies (PGAs), 
Direct Port Delivery, Installation of Container Sca nners, e -delivery orders, RFID based g ate-
automation System, etc. These initiatives have already been implemented at Jawaharlal Nehru 
Port Trust (JNPT) and are being taken up in other Major Ports. 
15.3 Lack of draft in some of the Major Ports has been an area of concern, which is hampering 
handling of larger vessels and consequently affecting the growth in cargo traffic. A great focus is 
being given on the issue of enhancing the draf t of ports. 10 of the 12 Major P orts have already 

31 
 
achieved a draft of 14 mtrs or above.  Steps are being taken to further increase the draft in the 
Major Ports so that they are able to handle larger vessels and are in a position to compete wi th 
major international leading Ports.

16.2 Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) implementation will improve the port operations as 
well as flow of information across all levels. Proposed system would aid in building a holistic 
port ecosystem that would improve the decision making process, help planning realistic future 
scenarios and increase performance and return-on-investment in the long run.

Major Issues Ailing Cargo Management in The Major Ports 
Draft Limitations 
Recommendation/Observation  
26. The Committee has observed that the relatively low draft at Indian P orts do not measure 
upto internationally set standards. Presently, vesse ls greater than 11,000 TEU are in service. 
The movement towards larger ships is driven by economics of scale. It follows that in case of 
containership for 1,000 TEU capacities, the average draft is 8.3 meter, which increases to 15.5 
metres for ships above 11,000 TEU capacities. Container vessels with a capacity of 4,000 TEU 
require a minimum draft of 12.5 meters.            (Para 223) 
27. The Committee feels that there is a need to maximize the utilization of these vessels, 
which will in turn lead to reduct ion in the number of port calls on major routes and push for the 
development of global mega ports served by fully integrated global network. Most Major Ports 

57 
 
in India have minimum draft under 12m, except for a few of the younger ports which have draft 
of more than 14m. Insufficient draft at Indian Ports leads to increased costs and time taken as 
cargo originating fro m and those that are bound for I ndia gets routed through tr ansshipment 
ports like Colombo and Singapore. The Committee feels that as vessels ke ep getting bigger, 
Indian ports need deeper drafts, which call for increased and greater investments in capital 
dredging.                 (Para 224) 
Reply of the Ministry 
27.1 Major capital dredging projects are proposed to be undertaken for increasing dra fts in 
Major Ports. In most of the Major Ports, 14 meters draft has been achieved except Kolkata Port 
where it is not feasible. Mormugao Port and Kamarajar Port Ltd. are b eing dredged to handle 18 
meter draft vessels, which are largest available  globally. At present, 18 meter d raft is available 
only in outer harbour of Visakhapatnam Port. 
Further recommendation/observation: 
27.2 The Committee is aware that drafts at Indian Ports have historically been low both 
in the channel and at berths. The Committee not es from the reply of the Ministry  that 14  
meter draft has been achieved in most of the Major Ports . C onsidering the fact that top 
container Ports in the world have achieved draft depth ranging from 14 m to 16 m long 
back and some Ports have enhanced this still further, there is a  need that draft for our 
Major Ports should be beyond 14 m in order to cater to the requirement of new generation 
ships. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Shipping should ensure 
that the Major Ports underta ke the dredging work to increase their draft dep th to 18 
meters within a definite  timeline. Since the dredging is highly capital intensive, the 
Committee would like to know as to how the Major Ports would meet their expenditure 
towards the capital and main tenance dredging and whether the dredging, if funded 
through internal resources and borrowings would entail the increase in their overall Port 
cost and consequently tariff.   
27.3 The Ministry should also provide reasons for the non -feasibility in implemen tation 
of major capital dredging p rojects at Kolkata Port. T he Committee would also like  the
